paras: The attempted lynching of W. S. Sanders occurred at Bunola, Pennsylvania, on Monday, August 17, 1903, when a crowd seized Sanders, a Black teamster accused of horsewhipping a white woman, and dragged him down the street amid cries of "Lynch him!" Officers rescued him and jailed him, and he was later reported to have pleaded guilty and been held for trial.

According to a dispatch dated Washington, Pennsylvania, a large crowd had gathered at the Monongahela wharf at Bunola, where a show boat was moored. Among them were Mrs. Mary E. Myers of Bunola, her young daughter, and Sanders, who worked as a teamster.

The dispatch said the girl began talking with Sanders and that her mother reproved her, "telling her to go away from the negro." In its account, Sanders, enraged, raised the heavy whip he carried and lashed Mrs. Myers about the face and body until she fainted. Bystanders then rushed Sanders and dragged him down the street by his legs, while cries of "Lynch him!" were heard "on every side." The dispatch said it "was feared that the negro would be summarily dealt with" before officers took him from the crowd and placed him in the borough prison.

At a hearing Sanders was reported to have pleaded guilty, and he was remanded to the county jail to await trial at court. Mrs. Myers was described as too badly injured to appear against him. No report of the trial or of any action against members of the crowd was found, and the dispatch names none of them.

The only report found ran in the Alexandria Gazette on August 19, 1903, under the headline "Negro Whips White Woman." The dispatch presented the whipping as fact, dwelt on the woman's injuries, and mentioned the crowd's lynching cries and the rescue without comment on the crowd. It identified Sanders by race throughout as "the negro" while naming no one in the crowd, and no coverage of the episode was found in the Black press.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of W. S. Sanders
bases: A crowd seized W. S. Sanders, accused of horsewhipping a white woman, dragged him down the street amid cries of 'Lynch him!' until officers rescued him and jailed him (A1).

The crowd of bystanders that seized Sanders acted without authority in response to an alleged assault, but officers rescued him and no one was killed (A1); this was an attempted or threatened lynching, not a lynching.
One dispatch dated Washington, Pa., Aug. 19, printed in the Alexandria Gazette, is the only report found in either press (A1).
